(2) An MEC may, with the concurrence of the Minister, delist an activity or area identified by the MEC.
(3) The Minister or MEC must follow the same public notice and comment procedure as for listing before delisting an activity or area.

title: Procedure for identifying competent authority
body:
(1) When listing or specifying activities, the Minister or MEC must identify the competent authority responsible for granting environmental authorisations for those activities.
(2) The Minister must be identified as the competent authority (unless otherwise agreed) if the activity has implications for international environmental commitments, has a development footprint spanning more than one province or crossing international boundaries, is undertaken by a national department or certain national organs of state, or will take place within a national protected area.
(2A) The Minister responsible for mineral resources must be identified as the competent authority where the activity is a mining activity.
(3) The Minister, the Minister responsible for mineral resources, and an MEC may agree that applications for certain activities may be dealt with by a different one of them than would otherwise apply.
(4)-(10) Where an MEC or the Minister responsible for mineral resources fails to take a decision within the prescribed time period, the applicant may apply to the Minister to facilitate or take the decision, following a notice and reporting process, with an annual report to Parliament on the exercise of this power.
(11)-(13) A person requiring authorisations under both this Act and a specific environmental management Act, or applying for a mining activity requiring an environmental authorisation, must submit those applications together; where the same authority decides both, an integrated decision must be issued.

title: Publication of list
body:
(1) The Minister or MEC must publish in the relevant Gazette a notice containing a list of activities or areas identified in terms of section 24(2), and competent authorities identified in terms of section 24C.
(2) The notice must specify the date on which the list comes into effect.

title: Minimum conditions attached to environmental authorisations
body: Every environmental authorisation must as a minimum ensure that adequate provision is made for the ongoing management and monitoring of the impacts of the activity on the environment throughout its life cycle, that the property, site or area is specified, and that provision is made for the transfer of rights and obligations.

title: Registration authorities
body:
(1) An association proposing to register its members as environmental assessment practitioners may apply to the Minister to be appointed as a registration authority.
(2) The application must contain the association's constitution, a list of its members, the criteria and process used to register practitioners, the qualifications of members responsible for assessing applicants, a code of conduct, and any other prescribed requirements.
(3) The Minister may, by notice in the Gazette, appoint the association as a registration authority, or refuse the application in writing with reasons.
(4) The Minister may, for good cause, terminate an association's appointment as a registration authority.
(5) The Minister must maintain a register of all associations appointed as registration authorities.
(6) The Minister may limit the number of registration authorities appointed, including to a single registration authority.

title: Appointment of external specialist to review assessment
body: The Minister or MEC may appoint an external specialist reviewer, and may recover the costs from the applicant, where the technical knowledge required to review any aspect of an assessment is not readily available within the competent authority, or a high level of objectivity not apparent in the submitted documents is required to determine whether the information is adequate for decision-making.

title: Implementation guidelines
body: The Minister or an MEC, with the concurrence of the Minister, may publish guidelines regarding listed activities or specified activities, or the implementation, administration and institutional arrangements of regulations made in terms of section 24(5).

title: Consultation between competent authorities
body:
(1) The Minister or an MEC may consult with any organ of state responsible for administering legislation relating to an activity that also requires environmental authorisation under this Act, in order to co-ordinate requirements and avoid duplication.
(2) The Minister or an MEC may enter into a written agreement with such an organ of state to avoid duplication in the submission of information or the carrying out of a process.
(3) The Minister or an MEC may consider such an agreement, and may take account of a process authorised under other legislation as adequate for meeting the requirements of Chapter 5, provided the core assessment requirements are given effect to.

title: Alignment of environmental authorisations
body:
(1) A competent authority empowered to issue an environmental authorisation and any other authority empowered under a specific environmental management Act may agree to issue an integrated environmental authorisation.
(2) An integrated environmental authorisation may be issued only if the relevant provisions of this Act and the other law have been complied with, and the authorisation specifies the provisions under which it was issued and the relevant authority or authorities that issued it.
(3) A competent authority may regard such an authorisation as sufficient basis for granting or refusing an authorisation under a specific environmental management Act it also administers.
(4) A competent authority may regard an authorisation under other legislation meeting all the relevant requirements as an environmental authorisation under Chapter 5.

title: Exemptions from application of certain provisions
body:
(1) The Minister or MEC may grant an exemption from any provision of this Act, except from the core assessment requirement or the requirement to obtain an environmental authorisation.
(2) The Minister responsible for mineral resources may grant an exemption from certain assessment requirements relating to mining.
(3) The Minister or MEC must prescribe the process for lodging and processing an exemption application.
(4) An exemption may only be granted if it is unlikely to result in significant detrimental consequences for the environment, the provision cannot be implemented in practice, it is unlikely to adversely affect the rights of interested or affected parties, or the activity is of national or provincial importance aimed at preventing or mitigating serious harm to the environment or property.

title: Environmental management programme
body:
(1) The Minister, the Minister responsible for mineral resources, or an MEC may require the submission of an environmental management programme before considering an application for an environmental authorisation, and must require it where an environmental impact assessment has been identified as the basis for the decision.
(2) The programme must contain prescribed information and, where appropriate, set time periods for implementation of measures, contain measures regulating responsibility for environmental damage, and include an environmental awareness plan.
(5)-(6) The relevant authority may call for additional information, direct that the programme be adjusted, or approve an amended programme after authorisation.
(7) The holder must give effect to the objectives in section 23, consider and manage all environmental impacts in accordance with the approved programme, monitor and audit compliance, rehabilitate the environment as far as reasonably practicable, and remains responsible for any environmental damage resulting from the operations.
(8) The directors of a company or members of a close corporation are jointly and severally liable for any negative impact on the environment caused by the entity they represent.

title: Criteria to be taken into account by competent authorities when considering applications
body:
(1) When considering an application for an environmental authorisation, the Minister, Minister responsible for mineral resources, or MEC must comply with this Act, and take into account relevant factors including any pollution or environmental degradation likely to result, mitigation measures, the applicant's ability to implement mitigation measures and comply with financial provision requirements, feasible alternatives, relevant maps and environmental management frameworks, information submitted in the application, comments from organs of state, and relevant guidelines and policies.
(2) The relevant authority or practitioner must consult with every organ of state that administers a law relating to a matter affecting the environment when considering the application.
(3) A consulted organ of state must submit comment within 30 days of being requested to do so in writing.

title: Incorporation of international environmental instruments
body:
(1) Where the Republic is not yet bound by an international environmental instrument, the Minister may make a recommendation to Cabinet and Parliament regarding accession to and ratification of that instrument, which may deal with available resources for implementation, views of interested and affected parties, benefits and disadvantages to the Republic, expected commencement dates, minimum accession requirements, departmental responsibilities, potential impact, and any reservations to be made.
(2) Where the Republic is a party to an international environmental instrument, the Minister, after compliance with section 231(2) and (3) of the Constitution, may publish the provisions of the instrument, and any amendment to it, in the Gazette.
(3) The Minister may introduce legislation or make regulations necessary to give effect to an international environmental instrument to which the Republic is a party, dealing with matters including co-ordination of implementation, allocation of responsibilities, information gathering and reporting, public participation, and compliance including offences and penalties.
(4) Before making a recommendation under subsection (1), the Minister may publish a notice in the Gazette stating the intention to do so and inviting written comments.

title: Reports
body:
(1) The Minister must report to Parliament once a year regarding international environmental instruments for which he or she is responsible, covering participation in international meetings, progress in implementing instruments the Republic is party to, preparations for likely future instruments, regional initiatives, the efficacy of co-ordination mechanisms, and legislative measures taken.
(2) The Minister must initiate an Annual Performance Report on Sustainable Development to meet the government's commitment to Agenda 21, covering the relevant activities of all national departments and spheres of government, to audit and report on performance, review co-ordination of policies and budgets, and review progress on public education in support of Agenda 21's objectives.

title: Application
body:
(1) This Chapter applies to any international environmental instrument whether the Republic became a party to it before or after this Act came into force.
(2) The provisions of any international environmental instrument published in accordance with this Chapter are evidence of the contents of that instrument in any proceedings or matter in which its provisions come into question.

title: Duty of care and remediation of environmental damage
body:
(1) Every person who causes, has caused or may cause significant pollution or degradation of the environment must take reasonable measures to prevent such pollution or degradation from occurring, continuing or recurring, or, in so far as such harm to the environment is authorised by law or cannot reasonably be avoided or stopped, to minimise and rectify such pollution or degradation of the environment.
(1A) Subsection (1) also applies to a significant pollution or degradation that-
(a) occurred before the commencement of this Act;
(b) arises or is likely to arise at a different time from the actual activity that caused the contamination; or
(c) arises through an act or activity of a person that results in a change to pre-existing contamination.
(2) Without limiting the generality of the duty in subsection (1), the persons on whom subsection (1) imposes an obligation to take reasonable measures, include an owner of land or premises, a person in control of land or premises or a person who has a right to use the land or premises on which or in which-
(a) any activity or process is or was performed or undertaken; or
(b) any other situation exists,
which causes, has caused or is likely to cause significant pollution or degradation of the environment.
(3) The measures required in terms of subsection (1) may include measures to-
(a) investigate, assess and evaluate the impact on the environment;
(b) inform and educate employees about the environmental risks of their work and the manner in which their tasks must be performed in order to avoid causing significant pollution or degradation of the environment;
(c) cease, modify or control any act, activity or process causing the pollution or degradation;
(d) contain or prevent the movement of pollutants or the causing of degradation;
(e) eliminate any source of the pollution or degradation; or
(f) remedy the effects of the pollution or degradation.
(4) The Director-General or a provincial head of department may, after consultation with any other organ of state concerned and after having given adequate opportunity to affected persons to inform him or her of their relevant interests, direct any person who fails to take the measures required under subsection (1) to-
(a) investigate, evaluate and assess the impact of specific activities and report thereon;
(b) commence taking specific reasonable measures before a given date;
(c) diligently continue with those measures; and
(d) complete them before a specified reasonable date:
Provided that the Director-General or a provincial head of department may, if urgent action is necessary for the protection of the environment, issue such directive, and consult and give such opportunity to inform as soon thereafter as is reasonable.
(5) The Director-General or a provincial head of department, when considering any measure or time period envisaged in subsection (4), must have regard to the principles set out in section 2, any adopted environmental management plan, the severity of any impact on the environment and the cost of the measures being considered, any measures proposed by the person on whom measures are to be imposed, the desirability of the State fulfilling its role as custodian holding the environment in public trust for the people, and any other relevant factors.
(6) If a person required to undertake rehabilitation or other remedial work on the land of another reasonably requires access to, use of, or a limitation on use of that land, but is unable to acquire it on reasonable terms, the Minister may expropriate the necessary rights for the benefit of the person undertaking the work, and recover the costs from the person for whose benefit the expropriation was effected.
(7) Should a person fail to comply, or inadequately comply, with a directive under subsection (4), the Director-General or provincial head of department may take reasonable measures to remedy the situation or apply to a competent court for appropriate relief.
(8) The Director-General or provincial head of department may recover costs for reasonable remedial measures from any person who caused or contributed to the pollution, the owner of the land at the relevant time or their successor in title, a person in control of or with a right to use the land at the relevant time, or any person who negligently failed to prevent the activity or situation, provided that person failed to take the measures required under subsection (1).
(9) The Director-General or provincial head of department may, in respect of recovery of costs under subsection (8), claim proportionally from any other person who benefited from the measures undertaken.
(10) Costs claimed under subsections (6), (8) and (9) must be reasonable and may include labour, administrative and overhead costs.
(11) Where more than one person is liable under subsection (8), liability must be apportioned according to the degree to which each was responsible for the harm.
(12) Any person may, after giving 30 days' notice, apply to a competent court for an order directing the Director-General or a provincial head of department to take steps under subsection (4), if they fail to do so.
(13) When considering such an application, the court must take into account the factors in subsection (5).
(14) No person may unlawfully and intentionally or negligently commit any act or omission which causes or is likely to cause significant pollution or degradation of the environment, detrimentally affects or is likely to affect the environment in a significant manner, or refuse to comply with a directive issued under this section.
(15) Any person who contravenes subsection (14) is guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding R1 million or imprisonment not exceeding 1 year, or both.

This is the most cited section of the whole Act, commonly referred to simply as "the section 28 duty of care." One known gap in this text: the 2022 Amendment Act extended who can issue directives under subsection (4) to also include municipalities, not just the Director-General and provincial heads of department shown here. If you are dealing with an actual pollution incident, confirm the current directive-issuing authority with a professional.

title: Protection of workers refusing to do environmentally hazardous work
body:
(1) Notwithstanding the provisions of any other law, no person is civilly or criminally liable or may be dismissed, disciplined, prejudiced or harassed on account of having refused to perform any work if the person in good faith and reasonably believed at the time of the refusal that the performance of the work would result in an imminent and serious threat to the environment.
(2) An employee who has refused to perform work in terms of subsection (1) must as soon thereafter as is reasonably practicable notify the employer either personally or through a representative that he or she has refused to perform work and give the reason for the refusal.
(3) Subsection (1) applies whether or not the person refusing to work has used or exhausted any other applicable external or internal procedure or otherwise remedied the matter concerned.
(4) No person may advantage or promise to advantage any person for not exercising his or her right in terms of subsection (1).
(5) No person may threaten to take any action contemplated by subsection (1) against a person because that person has exercised or intends to exercise his or her right in terms of subsection (1).

title: Control of emergency incidents
body:
(1) In this section-
"incident" means an unexpected sudden occurrence, including a major emission, fire or explosion, leading to serious danger to the public or potentially serious pollution of or detriment to the environment, whether immediate or delayed;
"responsible person" includes any person who is responsible for the incident, owns any hazardous substance involved in the incident, or was in control of any hazardous substance involved in the incident at the time of the incident;
"relevant authority" means a municipality with jurisdiction over the area in which an incident occurs, a provincial head of department (or other provincial official designated by the MEC) in a province where an incident occurs, the Director-General, or the relevant national or provincial authority responsible for administering any other law relevant to the incident.

The responsible person, or their employer if the incident occurred in the course of employment, must take immediate steps to contain and minimise the effects of the incident, undertake clean-up procedures, and remedy the effects of the incident. The responsible person must report the incident to the relevant authorities (including the Director-General, provincial head of department, and municipality) as soon as reasonably practicable, and must within 14 days submit a fuller written report on the nature of the incident, the substances involved, measures taken to mitigate its effects, the root cause, and steps taken to prevent a recurrence.

If a responsible person fails to comply, the relevant authority may take the necessary measures itself and recover its reasonable costs, jointly and severally, from every responsible person. When directing a responsible person to take specific measures within a set time, the relevant authority must have regard to the principles in section 2, the severity of the impact and cost of the measures, any measures already proposed by the responsible person, the desirability of the State fulfilling its role as custodian holding the environment in public trust, and any other relevant factors.

Note: this entry summarises section 30's key obligations from verified secondary legal sources rather than reproducing the complete verbatim text of every subsection, since the full text was not fully accessible when this entry was written. The Department has also published Guidelines on the Administration of Incidents to help distinguish a section 30 "incident" from a section 30A "emergency situation" (a related, separate provision allowing activities to proceed without an environmental authorisation in a genuine emergency). Confirm specific obligations with a professional if you are dealing with an actual incident.

title: Access to environmental information and protection of whistle-blowers
body:
This section protects anyone (including employees) who discloses information relating to an environmental risk, in good faith and reasonably believing they were disclosing evidence of that risk, from criminal or civil liability, and from being dismissed, disciplined, prejudiced, or harassed for making the disclosure. No person may threaten to take any of those actions against someone because they have exercised or intend to exercise this right.

A disclosure is protected if it is made to a parliamentary committee, an organ of state concerned with the environment or emergency services, the Public Protector, the Human Rights Commission, or an attorney-general.

A disclosure made to the media is also protected, but only where the person reasonably believed the disclosure was necessary to avert an imminent and serious threat to the environment, to ensure the threat was properly and timeously investigated, or to protect themselves against serious or irreparable harm from reprisals, or where the public interest in disclosure clearly outweighed any need for non-disclosure.

Note: this entry summarises section 31 from verified secondary legal sources rather than reproducing the complete verbatim text of every subsection, since the full text was not fully accessible when this entry was written. If you are considering making or responding to an environmental disclosure, confirm the exact current wording and any conditions with a professional.

title: Application
body:
(1) This Part applies to the enforcement of this Act and the specific environmental management Acts.
(2) In this Part, unless inconsistent with the context, a word or expression to which a meaning has been assigned in a specific environmental management Act has, in relation to the administration or enforcement of that Act, the meaning assigned to it in that Act.
(3) For the purposes of this Part, Schedule 1 to the Criminal Procedure Act, 1977 (Act No. 51 of 1977), is deemed to include an offence committed in terms of this Act or a specific environmental management Act.

title: Designation of environmental management inspectors by Minister
body:
(1) The Minister may-
(a) designate as an environmental management inspector, any staff member of the Department or any other organ of state; and
(b) at any time withdraw a designation made in terms of paragraph (a).
(2) A designation in terms of subsection (1)(a)(ii) may only be made by agreement between the Minister and the relevant organ of state.

Note: since this section was inserted, further sections (31BA and 31BB) have been added to allow the Minister responsible for water affairs, and the Minister responsible for mineral resources, to also designate environmental management inspectors for matters within their portfolios - those two sections are not yet reproduced in this app.

title: Designation of environmental management inspectors by MEC
body:
(1) An MEC may-
(a) designate as an environmental management inspector, any staff member of the department responsible for environmental management in the province, any other provincial organ of state, or any municipality in the province; and
(b) at any time withdraw a designation made in terms of paragraph (a).
(2) A designation in terms of subsection (1)(a)(ii) or (iii) may only be made by agreement between the relevant MEC and the relevant provincial organ of state or municipality.

title: Mandates
body:
(1) When designating a person as an environmental management inspector, the Minister or MEC must determine whether the person concerned is designated for the enforcement of this Act, a specific environmental management Act, specific provisions of this Act or a specific environmental management Act, this Act and all specific environmental management Acts, or any combination of those Acts or provisions.
(2) An MEC may designate a person as an environmental management inspector only for the enforcement of provisions administered by the MEC or a provincial organ of state, or in respect of which the MEC or a provincial organ of state exercises assigned or delegated powers or duties.
(3) A designated inspector may exercise any of the powers given to environmental management inspectors in terms of this Act that are necessary for the inspector's mandate and that are specified by the Minister or MEC by notice in writing.

title: Prescribed standards
body:
(1) The Minister may prescribe qualification criteria for environmental management inspectors, and training that must be completed by them.
(2) The Minister may only prescribe criteria and training after consultation with the Minister responsible for safety and security.

title: Proof of designation
body:
(1) A prescribed identity card must be issued to each person designated as an environmental management inspector.
(2) When exercising any powers or performing any duties, an environmental management inspector must, on demand by a member of the public, produce the identity card and the written notice of mandate.

title: Functions of inspectors
body:
(1) An environmental management inspector, within their mandate, must monitor and enforce compliance with the law for which they have been designated, and may investigate any act or omission reasonably suspected of constituting an offence, a breach of that law, or a breach of a permit, authorisation, or other instrument issued under it.
(2) An environmental management inspector must carry out duties in accordance with instructions issued by the Minister or MEC and any prescribed procedures, may be accompanied by an interpreter or other assistant, and must exercise powers in a way that minimises any damage, loss, or deterioration to premises or property.

title: General powers
body: An environmental management inspector, within their mandate, may question a person about a suspected offence or breach, issue a written notice requiring a person who refuses to answer to do so, inspect and copy or remove documents and records, require documents to be produced, inspect and remove items reasonably suspected of being used in an offence, take photographs or recordings, dig or bore into soil, take samples, remove unlawfully deposited waste, and carry out other prescribed duties. A person who receives a written notice to answer questions must answer truthfully, though an incriminating answer may not be used against them in later criminal proceedings for the same offence. An inspector must provide a receipt for anything removed and return it within a reasonable period. Inspectors also have all the powers assigned to a police official who is not a commissioned officer under Chapters 2, 5, 7 and 8 of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1977.

title: Seizure of items
body:
(1) The disposal provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1977 apply to items seized under this Part.
(2) An inspector may request the person previously in control of a seized item to take it to a designated place, or may do so themselves if the person refuses.
(3) A seized vehicle, vessel, or aircraft may be immobilised by removing a part.
(4) Seized items must be kept secure against damage.
(5) For imported or exported specimens of threatened or protected species, an inspector may require the responsible person to produce the original import or export permit and supporting documentation.

title: Powers to stop, enter and search vehicles, vessels and aircraft
body:
(1) An environmental management inspector, within their mandate, may without a warrant enter and search any vehicle, vessel, aircraft, or pack-animal reasonably suspected of being used to commit an offence or breach, or of containing evidence of one.
(2) An inspector may, without a warrant, seize anything found that may serve as evidence.
(4) An inspector may, without a warrant, order a driver to stop or a pilot to land, and if necessary force them to do so.
(6) An inspector may apply to the National or Provincial Commissioner of Police for written authorisation to establish a roadblock or checkpoint, and has, within their mandate, all the powers of a police member under section 13(8) of the South African Police Service Act, 1995 for that purpose.

title: Routine inspections
body:
(1) An environmental management inspector, within their mandate, may at any reasonable time, without a warrant, enter and inspect any building, land, or premises (other than residential premises) to check compliance with the relevant law or a permit condition.
(2)-(3) An inspector may enter and inspect residential premises only with a warrant issued by a magistrate on written application under oath, setting out that it is necessary for ascertaining compliance.
(4) An inspector may enter residential premises without a warrant if the person in control consents, or if there are reasonable grounds to believe a warrant would be granted but the delay of applying for one would defeat the purpose.
(5) While carrying out a routine inspection, an inspector may seize anything that may be used as evidence.

title: Power to issue compliance notices
body:
(1) An environmental management inspector, within their mandate, may issue a compliance notice in the prescribed form if there are reasonable grounds to believe a person has not complied with the relevant law or a permit condition.
(2) A compliance notice must set out the details of the non-compliance, any steps the person must take and the period for doing so, anything the person may not do, and the procedure for objecting to the notice.
(3) An inspector may, on good cause shown, vary a notice and extend the compliance period.
(4)-(5) A person must comply with the notice within the stated time unless the Minister or MEC agrees to suspend it pending an objection.

title: Objections to compliance notice
body:
(1) A person who receives a compliance notice may object by making written representations to the Minister or MEC within 30 days of receipt, or a longer period if allowed.
(2) After considering the representations, the Minister or MEC may confirm, modify, or cancel the notice, and must specify the period for compliance with any part that is confirmed or modified.

title: Failure to comply with compliance notice
body:
(1) Failing to comply with a compliance notice is an offence.
(2) The inspector must report the non-compliance to the Minister or MEC, who may revoke or vary the relevant permit or authorisation, take necessary steps and recover the costs from the person who failed to comply, and report the matter to a Director of Public Prosecutions.

title: Powers of South African Police Service members
body:
(1) A member of the South African Police Service has, for offences under this Act or a specific environmental management Act, all the powers of an environmental management inspector under this Part, excluding routine inspections and issuing or enforcing compliance notices.
(2) The Minister or MEC may, with the concurrence of the Minister responsible for safety and security, assign those excluded powers to a specific police member by written notice.

title: Duty to produce documents
body: Any person to whom a permit, licence, permission, certificate, authorisation, or other document has been issued under this Act or a specific environmental management Act must produce that document at the request of an environmental management inspector.

title: Confidentiality
body:
(1) It is an offence to disclose information about another person acquired while exercising a power or duty under this Act or a specific environmental management Act, except where disclosure is required by law, ordered by a court, necessary to enable a person to perform a function under this Act, or for the purposes of the administration of justice.
(2) A person convicted of this offence is liable to a fine or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both.

title: Offences relating to environmental management inspectors
body:
(1) A person commits an offence if they hinder or interfere with an environmental management inspector performing official duties, pretend to be an inspector or their interpreter or assistant, furnish false or misleading information when complying with an inspector's request, or fail to comply with such a request.
(2) A person convicted of this offence is liable to a fine or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both.

title: Award of part of fine recovered to informant
body:
(1) A court imposing a fine for an offence under this Act or a specific environmental management Act may order that up to one-fourth of the fine be paid to the person whose evidence led to the conviction or who helped bring the offender to justice.
(2) A person employed by an organ of state or otherwise engaged in implementing this Act is not entitled to such an award.

title: Cancellation of permits
body: The court convicting a person of an offence under this Act or a specific environmental management Act may withdraw any permit or authorisation abused by that person, disqualify them from obtaining a permit or authorisation for up to five years, and order that all competent authorities be notified of the disqualification.

title: Forfeiture of items
body:
(1) A convicting court may declare any specimen, container, vehicle, vessel, aircraft, or document used in connection with the offence and seized under this Part to be forfeited to the State.
(3) Any forfeited specimen must be repatriated to its country of export or origin at the convicted person's expense, deposited in an appropriate institution or museum, or otherwise appropriately disposed of.

title: Treatment of seized live specimens
body: Pending criminal proceedings, a live specimen seized under this Part must be deposited with a suitable institution, rescue centre, or facility able and willing to house and care for it properly.

title: Security for release of vehicles, vessels or aircraft
body:
(1) The owner or agent of a seized vehicle, vessel, or aircraft being kept for criminal proceedings may apply to a court for its release.
(2) A court may order release on provision of security.
(3) The security must at least equal the vehicle's market value, the maximum fine for the alleged offence, and the State's costs of prosecuting it.
(4) The court may order release on a lesser amount of security if satisfied there are circumstances warranting it.

title: Admission of guilt fines
body:
(1) The Minister may by regulation specify offences for which alleged offenders may pay a prescribed admission of guilt fine instead of going to court.
(2) An inspector who reasonably believes such an offence was committed may issue a written notice under section 56 of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1977.
(3) The fine may not exceed the prescribed amount or what a court would likely have imposed.

title: Delegation of powers and duties by Minister and Director-General
body:
(1) The Minister may delegate a power or duty under this Act or a specific environmental management Act to the Director-General, an MEC (by agreement), the management authority of a protected area, or any organ of state (by agreement).
(2) A delegation must be in writing, may be made subject to conditions, does not prevent the Minister exercising the power personally, may include the power to subdelegate, and may be withdrawn.
(2C) The Minister may not delegate the power to make regulations, publish notices in the Gazette, appoint a board or committee member, or expropriate private land.
(3) The Director-General may delegate a power or duty to an official in the Department, or after consultation with a provincial head of department, to a provincial or municipal officer.

title: Delegation of powers by MEC
body:
(1) An MEC may delegate a power or duty to the head of their department, the management authority of a provincial or local protected area, a municipality (by agreement), or any provincial organ of state (by agreement).
(2) A delegation must be in writing, may be subject to conditions, does not prevent the MEC exercising the power personally, may include the power to subdelegate, and may be withdrawn.
(4) An MEC may not delegate the power to make regulations, publish notices in the Gazette, appoint a board or committee member, or expropriate private land.

title: Regulations, legal documents and steps valid under certain circumstances
body:
(1) A regulation, notice, authorisation, permit, or other document that does not comply with a procedural requirement is nevertheless valid if the non-compliance is not material and does not prejudice any person, and may be corrected without following the usual procedure if the correction does not materially change anyone's rights and duties.
(2) A failure to take a required step before a decision does not invalidate that decision if the failure is not material, does not prejudice any person, and is not procedurally unfair.

title: Consultation
body: A requirement to consult a person or organ of state is regarded as satisfied if formal written notification of the intended action was given and no response was received within a reasonable time.

title: Extension of time periods
body: The Minister or an MEC may extend, or condone a failure to comply with, a time period under this Act or a specific environmental management Act, except a period that binds the Minister or MEC themselves.

title: Delivery of documents
body:
(1) A notice or document may be delivered by hand, by registered mail to the person's business or residential address (or a juristic person's registered address), or, where the address is unknown despite reasonable enquiry, by publishing it once in the Gazette and once in a local newspaper.
(2) A document delivered by registered mail or published is regarded as having come to the person's notice unless the contrary is proved.

title: Limitation of liability
body: Neither the State nor any other person is liable for damage or loss caused by the exercise of, or failure to exercise, a power or duty under this Act or a specific environmental management Act, unless that exercise or failure was unlawful, negligent, or in bad faith.

title: Legal standing to enforce environmental laws
body:
(1) Any person or group of persons may seek appropriate relief in respect of any breach or threatened breach of any provision of this Act, including a principle contained in Chapter 1, or of any provision of a specific environmental management Act, or of any other statutory provision concerned with the protection of the environment or the use of natural resources.
(2) A court may decide not to award costs against a person or group who fails to secure the relief sought, if the court considers they acted reasonably out of concern for the public interest or to protect the environment, and made due efforts to use other means reasonably available to obtain that relief.
(3) Where a person or group secures the relief sought, a court may on application make further appropriate orders.

title: Financial provision for remediation of environmental damage
body:
(1) An applicant for an environmental authorisation relating to prospecting, mining, exploration, production or related activities must make the prescribed financial provision for the rehabilitation, management and closure of environmental impacts, before the Minister of Minerals and Energy issues the environmental authorisation.
(2) If a holder fails to rehabilitate or manage an environmental impact, or is unable to, the Minister of Minerals and Energy may, upon written notice, use all or part of the financial provision to rehabilitate or manage the impact.
(3) Every holder must annually assess their environmental liability and adjust their financial provision if circumstances require it.
(5) The requirement to maintain the financial provision remains in force until the Minister issues a closure certificate, though a portion may be retained for latent or residual impacts.

title: Monitoring and performance assessment
body: As part of the general terms and conditions for an environmental authorisation, and in order to ensure compliance with its conditions and assess the continued adequacy of the environmental management programme, every holder must conduct such monitoring and performance assessment as may be prescribed.

title: Mine closure on environmental authorisation
body:
(1) Every holder remains responsible for any environmental liability, pollution, ecological degradation, and the pumping and treatment of extraneous water, until the Minister of Minerals and Energy has issued a closure certificate under the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act, 2002.
(2) When issuing a closure certificate, the Minister must return the appropriate portion of the financial provision, but may retain a portion for any latent or residual environmental impact that may emerge later.
(3) Every holder must plan, manage and implement mine closure procedures as prescribed.

title: Private prosecution
body:
(1) Any person may, in the public interest or in the interest of the protection of the environment, institute and conduct a prosecution in respect of any breach or threatened breach of any duty (other than a public duty resting on an organ of state) in any national or provincial legislation or municipal by-law, or any regulation, licence, permission or authorisation issued under such legislation, where that duty concerns the protection of the environment and the breach is an offence.
(2) The private prosecution provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1977 apply, provided the person prosecuting does so through an admitted advocate or attorney, has given the public prosecutor written notice of their intent, and the public prosecutor has not, within 28 days, stated an intention to prosecute - in which case a certificate of refusal to prosecute and security for costs are not required.
(3) A court may order a person convicted on private prosecution to pay the costs and expenses of the prosecution.
(4) The accused may be granted a costs order against the private prosecutor if the charge is dismissed, the accused acquitted, or a favourable decision given on appeal, and the court finds the prosecution was not brought out of genuine concern for the public interest or the environment, or was unfounded, trivial, or vexatious.
(5) Once a private prosecution has been instituted, the Attorney-General may not prosecute except with leave of the court.

title: Criminal proceedings
body:
(1) Where a person is convicted of an offence under a provision listed in Schedule 3 and appears to have caused loss or damage (including rehabilitation costs) to an organ of state or other person, the court may, at the written request of the Minister or the affected party, and in the convicted person's presence, summarily inquire into the amount of that loss or damage.
(2) On proof of that amount, the court may give judgment for it in favour of the organ of state or person concerned, enforceable as a civil judgment.
(3) The court may also summarily assess the monetary value of any advantage gained by the offence and order payment of damages, compensation, or a fine equal to that amount, in addition to any other punishment.
(4) The court may order the convicted person to pay the reasonable investigation and prosecution costs incurred by the public prosecutor and the organ of state.
(5) An employer is guilty of an offence committed by a manager, agent, or employee acting (or failing to act) on the employer's behalf, if the employer failed to take all reasonable steps to prevent it - proof of the act by the manager, agent, or employee is prima facie evidence of the employer's guilt.
(6) The manager, agent, or employee themselves may also be convicted and sentenced as if they were the employer.
(7) A director of a firm at the time of an offence by that firm is themselves guilty of the offence if it resulted from the director's failure to take reasonable steps to prevent it, unless they can rebut this.
(8) Such a manager, agent, employee, or director may be convicted in addition to the employer or firm.
(10) The Minister may amend Part (a) of Schedule 3 by regulation; an MEC may amend Part (b) for their province.

title: Conclusion of agreements
body:
(1) The Minister, every MEC, and every municipality may enter into environmental management co-operation agreements with any person or community to promote compliance with the principles of this Act.
(2) Such agreements may only be entered into with the agreement of every organ of state with jurisdiction over the relevant activity, and the Minister and MEC concerned, after complying with prescribed public participation procedures, and must comply with any regulations prescribed under section 45.
(3) An agreement may contain an undertaking by the person or community to improve on the legal standards applicable to it, measurable targets and dates for meeting that undertaking, provision for monitoring, independent verification and inspection, and measures for non-compliance including penalties and incentives.

title: Expropriation
body:
(1) The Minister may purchase, or (subject to compensation) expropriate, any property for an environmental or other purpose under this Act, if that purpose is a public purpose or in the public interest, consulting the Minister of Minerals and Energy first if mineral rights are involved.
(2) The Expropriation Act, 1975 applies to expropriations under this Act.
(3) Compensation, and the time and manner of payment, must be determined in accordance with section 25(3) of the Constitution, and the owner must be given a hearing before expropriation.

title: Reservation
body: The Minister may reserve State land, with the consent of the Minister authorised to dispose of that land and after consulting any other relevant Minister, for environmental or other purposes under this Act, if that purpose is a public purpose or in the public interest.

title: Intervention in litigation
body: The Minister may intervene in litigation before a court in any matter arising under this Act.

title: Agreements
body: The Director-General may enter into agreements with organs of state in order to fulfil their responsibilities under this Act.

title: Appointment of employees on contract
body:
(1) The Director-General may appoint employees on contract outside the Public Service Act, 1994, when necessary to carry out the Department's functions.
(2) The Director-General must, after consulting the Department of Public Service and Administration, determine the conditions of employment for such employees.
(3) Such employees are remunerated from money appropriated by Parliament for that purpose.

title: Assignment of powers
body:
(1) In this section, "assignment" means an assignment as contemplated in section 99 of the Constitution.
(2) The Minister must record all such assignments in a Schedule to this Act, and may amend that Schedule.

title: Appeals
body:
(1) Any affected person may appeal to the Minister against a decision taken by a person acting under a power delegated by the Minister under this Act.
(2) An appeal must be noted and dealt with in the prescribed manner.

title: Regulations in general
body:
(1) The Minister may make regulations dealing with any matter this Act requires to be dealt with by regulation, and generally to carry out the Act's purposes and provisions.
(2) The Minister may make different regulations for different activities, provinces, geographical areas, and owners or classes of owners of land.
(3) The Minister may, by regulation, make infringement of certain regulations a criminal offence and prescribe penalties for it.

title: Regulations for management co-operation agreements
body:
(1) The Minister may make regulations covering procedures for concluding environmental management co-operation agreements (including public participation), their duration, information requirements, general conditions and prohibitions, reporting, and monitoring and inspection.
(2) An MEC or municipal council may substitute their own regulations or by-laws for the Minister's, provided they cover the same matters and comply with this Act's principles.

title: Model environmental management by-laws
body:
(1) The Minister may make model by-laws for managing the environmental impacts of development within a municipality's jurisdiction, which a municipality may adopt as its own by-laws.
(2) A municipality may ask the Director-General for help preparing environmental by-laws, and the Director-General may not unreasonably refuse.
(4) The purpose of model by-laws is to mitigate adverse environmental impacts, facilitate implementation of authorisation decisions and conditions, and ensure effective environmental management and conservation within the municipality's jurisdiction.
(5) Model by-laws must include measures for auditing, monitoring, ensuring compliance, and reporting.

title: Procedure for making regulations
body:
(1) Before making regulations, a Minister or MEC must publish a notice in the relevant Gazette setting out the draft regulations and inviting written comment within a specified period, and must consider all comments received.
(2) The Minister must table any new regulations in Parliament (National Assembly and National Council of Provinces) within 30 days of promulgation; an MEC must table them in the relevant provincial legislature.
(3) A parliamentary or provincial committee must consider and report on whether the regulations are consistent with this Act's purposes, within the powers it confers, consistent with the Constitution, and create appropriate offences and penalties.
(4)-(5) The National Council of Provinces, National Assembly, or a provincial legislature may reject or disapprove regulations by resolution within specified periods, though a disapproval can be suspended to allow the defect to be corrected.
(6) A disapproved regulation lapses, without affecting anything validly done under it, or rights, privileges, obligations, or liabilities already incurred, before it lapsed.

title: State bound
body: This Act binds the State, except as regards criminal liability.

title: Repeal of laws
body:
(1) Sections 2 to 15, 27A, and 38 of the Environment Conservation Act, 1989 are repealed.
(2) Sections 21, 22, and 26 of the Environment Conservation Act, 1989, and the notices and regulations issued under sections 21 and 22 and in force when this Act commenced, are repealed with effect from a date the Minister publishes in the Gazette, which may not be earlier than when equivalent regulations or notices under section 24 of this Act have been promulgated and the Minister is satisfied the old ones have become redundant.

title: Savings
body: Anything done, or considered to have been done, under a provision repealed by this Act remains valid to the extent it is consistent with this Act, until something done under this Act overrides it, and is otherwise considered to be an action under the corresponding provision of this Act.

title: Short title
body: This Act is called the National Environmental Management Act, 1998.

title: Commencement
body: This Act comes into operation on a date fixed by the President in the Gazette.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Employer to conduct occupational hygiene measurements
body:
(1) The employer must engage the part-time or full-time services of a person qualified in occupational hygiene techniques to measure levels of exposure to hazards at the mine if required to do so by regulation or a notice in the Gazette, or if, after assessing risks in terms of section 11(1), it is necessary to do so.
(2) Every system of occupational hygiene measurements must be appropriate, considering the hazards to which the employees are or may be exposed, and be designed so that it provides information the employer can use in determining measures to eliminate, control and minimise the health risks and hazards to which employees are or may be exposed.
(3) The employer must keep a record of all occupational hygiene measurements in a manner that can be linked as far as practicable to each employee's record of medical surveillance.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Employer to establish system of medical surveillance
body:
(1) The employer must establish and maintain a system of medical surveillance of employees exposed to health hazards if required to do so by regulation or a notice in the Gazette, or if, after assessing risks in terms of section 11(1), it is necessary to do so.
(2) Every system of medical surveillance must be appropriate, be designed to provide information the employer can use to eliminate, control and minimise health risks or prevent, detect and treat occupational diseases, and consist of an initial medical examination and other medical examinations at appropriate intervals.
(3) An employer establishing such a system must engage an occupational medical practitioner, supply them with the means to perform their functions, and keep a record of medical surveillance for each employee exposed to a health hazard.
(4A) The employer must inform the Principal Inspector of Mines, in writing, within seven days of appointing an occupational medical practitioner, including their name, practice number, and whether engaged full or part time.
(5) An occupational medical practitioner must take every reasonably practicable measure to promote the health and safety of employees and assist them in matters related to occupational medicine.
(6) If an employee is declared unfit due to an occupational disease, the employer must conduct an investigation under section 11(5).
(7) If an employee is temporarily unfit but expected to recover, the practitioner must record and notify both employer and employee of that fact.
(8) The employer must retain relevant records until the mine closes, then deliver them to the Medical Inspector.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Record of hazardous work
body:
(1) The employer at every mine must keep a service record, in the prescribed form, of employees who perform work in respect of which medical surveillance is conducted under section 13.
(2) The employer must deliver to the Medical Inspector a copy of the relevant part of the record when an employee whose name appears in it ceases to be employed at that mine, or when required to do so by the Chief Inspector of Mines.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Record of medical surveillance
body:
(1) An employee's record of medical surveillance must be kept confidential and may only be made available in accordance with the ethics of medical practice, if required by law or court order, or if the employee has consented in writing.
(2) Any person required to maintain such a record must store it safely, and not destroy or dispose of it for 40 years from the last date of medical surveillance of that employee.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Annual medical reports
body:
(1) Every occupational medical practitioner at a mine must compile an annual report covering employees at that mine, giving an analysis of their health based on medical surveillance records, without disclosing employee names.
(2) The report must be given to the employer, who must deliver a copy to the health and safety committee (or representatives, if there is no committee) and to the Medical Inspector.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Exit certificates
body:
(1) If an employee subject to medical surveillance has their employment terminated, the employer must arrange an exit medical examination.
(2) The examination must be held before, or within 30 days after, termination of employment.
(3) The employee must attend the examination.
(4) The occupational medical practitioner conducting it must produce an exit certificate indicating the results of all medical surveillance and the presence or absence of any occupational disease, and enter a copy into the employee's record of medical surveillance.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Costs of examination
body: The employer must pay the costs of all clinical examinations and medical tests performed in terms of this Act unless this Act expressly provides otherwise.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Employees' right to information
body:
(1) An employee may request, and the employer must then provide, a copy of the record or part of it that is kept in terms of sections 12(3) and 13(3)(c) and relates to that employee.
(2) The occupational medical practitioner conducting an exit examination must provide the employee with a copy of the exit certificate prepared as a result.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Employee may dispute finding of unfitness to perform work
body:
(1) An employee may appeal to the Medical Inspector against a decision that they are unfit to perform a particular category of work, or any finding in an exit certificate.
(2) An appeal must be lodged within 30 days of the decision or finding, or such further period as prescribed, and must state the grounds of appeal.
(3) The Medical Inspector must choose a medical practitioner not employed by the employer to re-examine the employee, at the cost of the Chief Inspector of Mines.
(4) That practitioner reports to the Medical Inspector, who then confirms, sets aside, varies, or substitutes the original decision or finding.
(5) Nothing precludes the employee from obtaining their own medical opinion at their own cost, or pursuing any other legal remedy.
(6) "Employee" for this section includes any applicant for employment previously employed at a mine.
(7) An employee lodging an appeal may not be dismissed on grounds relating to unfitness to perform work, pending the outcome of the appeal.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Manufacturer's and supplier's duty for health and safety
body:
(1) Anyone who designs, manufactures, repairs, imports, or supplies any article for use at a mine must ensure, as far as reasonably practicable, that it is safe when used properly and complies with this Act; anyone who erects or installs an article must ensure the manner of erection or installation doesn't make it unsafe; and anyone who designs, manufactures, erects, or installs an article must ensure ergonomic principles are considered.
(2) A person's duty under subsection (1) is relieved to the extent reasonable if another person provides a written undertaking to take sufficient steps to ensure the article's safety and compliance.
(3) Anyone who designs or constructs a building or structure (including temporary) for mine use must ensure, as far as reasonably practicable, that it is safe when used properly.
(4) Every person who manufactures, imports, or supplies a hazardous substance for mine use must ensure it is safe when properly used, handled, processed, stored, or transported, and provide adequate information on its use, risks, restrictions, safety precautions, emergency procedures, and disposal, complying with the Hazardous Substances Act, 1973.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Employees' duties for health and safety
body: Every employee at a mine, while at that mine, must take reasonable care to protect their own health and safety and that of others affected by their acts or omissions, use and care for protective clothing and equipment provided, report promptly to their supervisor any situation presenting a risk they cannot properly deal with, co-operate to permit compliance with duties under this Act, and comply with prescribed health and safety measures.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Employees' right to leave dangerous working place
body:
(1) An employee has the right to leave any working place whenever circumstances arise which, with reasonable justification, appear to pose a serious danger to their health or safety, or when directed to leave by the responsible health and safety representative.
(2) The employer, after consulting the health and safety committee, must determine effective procedures for exercising this right, covering notification, participation in resolving issues, assignment to alternative work, and notifying other employees of the refusal and its reason.
(3) If there is no committee, consultation must be with health and safety representatives, or employees if there is no representative.
(4) The Minister must, by notice in the Gazette, determine minimum requirements for these procedures.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Employees not to pay for safety measures
body: No person may make any deduction from an employee's wages, or permit an employee to make any payment to any person, in respect of anything the employer is obliged to provide or do in terms of this Act in the interest of the health and safety of an employee.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Negotiations and consultations before appointment of representatives
body:
(1) The employer of a mine requiring health and safety representatives must meet, within the prescribed period, with the representative trade union to negotiate a collective agreement covering the designation of working places, the number of full-time representatives, their election/appointment, terms of office, vacancy procedures, functions, procedures for the right to withdraw from danger, meeting arrangements, facilities and assistance, training, dispute resolution, and other relevant matters.
(2) Before concluding such an agreement, the employer must consult all other registered trade unions with members at the mine.
(6)-(7) If there is no representative trade union, the employer must consult with the registered trade unions, or with employees/their representatives if there is no registered trade union, and endeavour to reach agreement on the number of full-time representatives.
(8)-(11) If no agreement is reached, a dispute exists, which may be referred to the Commission for conciliation, and then arbitration if unresolved, with the Commission determining the number of representatives taking Schedule 1's guidelines into account.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Designation of working places
body:
(1) If a collective agreement is concluded, the employer must designate working places in accordance with it.
(2) If no agreement is concluded, the employer must designate working places so that every working place is designated, no representative is responsible for more than 100 employees, and no representative is responsible for more than 50 employees if the designated working place includes separate working places.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Qualifications of representatives
body:
(1) To qualify as a health and safety representative, an employee must be employed full-time in the designated working place and be acquainted with conditions and activities there.
(2) To qualify as a full-time representative, an employee must be employed full-time at the mine and comply with any other qualifications agreed by a health and safety committee or prescribed.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Election and appointment of representatives
body:
(1) Employees in a designated working place may elect health and safety representatives from among themselves.
(2) Employees at the mine may elect any agreed full-time representatives from among themselves.
(3) Elections must be conducted in the prescribed manner.
(4) Employees selected must be appointed by the employer in the prescribed manner.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Rights and powers of representatives
body:
(1) A health and safety representative may represent employees on health and safety matters, direct an employee to leave a dangerous working place, assist an employee who has left one, identify hazards, make representations to the employer or committee, inspect relevant documents, request information from an inspector, consult an adviser with employer approval, attend relevant committee meetings, request investigations or inquiries, participate in consultations and inspections, investigate complaints, examine accident causes, visit accident sites, attend post-accident inspections, co-operate in investigations, participate in inquiries, and perform agreed or prescribed functions.
(2) These rights apply only to the working places for which the representative is responsible.
(3)-(7) An inspector must supply requested information; employer approval for advisers may not be unreasonably withheld; representatives are entitled to perform functions and receive training during ordinary working hours, treated as employment duties.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Duty to compensate and assist representatives
body:
(1) The employer must pay every full-time health and safety representative remuneration at least equal to what they earned before appointment.
(2) The employer must provide reasonable time and facilities for monthly meetings between employees and their representatives.
(3) The employer must provide representatives with necessary facilities and assistance, required training, and paid time off for agreed or prescribed training courses.
(4) This assistance does not include costs of advisers or independent experts unless otherwise agreed.
(5) On completing a term as full-time representative, the representative is entitled to their previous position, or one at least as favourable.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Duty to inform representatives
body: Every employer must notify the relevant health and safety representatives, and the employee co-chairperson of the committee if there is one, in good time of inspections, investigations, or inquiries the employer has been notified of, and as soon as practicable of any accident, serious illness, health-threatening occurrence, or other dangerous event.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Negotiation and consultation on establishment of committees
body:
(1) The employer of a mine requiring a health and safety committee must meet, within the prescribed period, with the representative trade union to negotiate a collective agreement on the number of committees and their responsibility, representative numbers, election/appointment, terms of office, vacancy filling, meeting arrangements, facilities, and dispute resolution procedure.
(2) Before concluding this agreement, the employer must consult all other registered trade unions with members at the mine.
(6)-(7) If there is no representative trade union, the employer must consult registered trade unions, or employees/their representatives if none, within the prescribed period.
(8) These negotiations may be held together with those under section 26.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Establishment of health and safety committees
body:
(1) If a collective agreement is concluded under section 33(1), committees must be established in terms of it.
(2) If no agreement is concluded, the employer must establish committees after the required consultation, in accordance with this section and regulations.
(3) A committee must consist of at least four employee representatives and no more employer representatives than employee representatives.
(4) Health and safety representatives appoint the employee representatives, who must be broadly representative of the mine's working places and be employees there.
(5) No more than two employee representatives may be non-representative full-time employees, unless all representatives are already on the committee.
(6) The employer appoints the employer representatives, who must include persons with authority to develop and implement health and safety policies.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Committee procedures
body:
(1) Employee and employer representatives must each elect a chairperson from their number, alternating as presiding chairperson unless otherwise agreed.
(2) The committee must meet at least once a month, unless otherwise agreed.
(3) A committee may determine its own rules and procedures.
(4) Others may be invited to attend meetings and participate.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Rights and powers of health and safety committee
body:
(1) A health and safety committee may represent employees on health and safety matters, participate in consultations on scheduled matters, request the Chief Inspector of Mines to review a code of practice, request relevant information, agree additional representative qualifications or functions, request investigations or inquiries, consult an adviser with employer approval, and take reasonable time to prepare for and report on meetings.
(2) Employer approval for advisers may not be unreasonably withheld.
(3)-(4) Committee members are entitled to perform functions and receive training during ordinary working hours, treated as employment duties.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Duty to support committee
body: The employer must provide the health and safety committee with facilities and assistance reasonably necessary to perform its functions, and supply it with the annual report referred to in section 2(1)(c) and any information necessary to perform its functions.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Disclosure of information
body:
(1) When required to supply information to a representative or committee, an employer, inspector, or inquiry presider must not disclose private personal information about an employee without their written consent, and need not supply legally privileged information, information they are prohibited from disclosing by law or court order, or confidential information that could cause substantial harm if disclosed.
(2) An employee may not unreasonably withhold consent to disclosure of their own information.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Disputes concerning disclosure of information
body:
(1) A dispute about required disclosure may be referred in writing to the Commission by any party.
(3) The Commission must attempt conciliation.
(4) If unresolved, arbitration may be requested.
(5)-(6) An arbitrator must first decide if disclosure is required, then, for sensitive information, balance the harm of disclosure against the harm of non-disclosure to representatives' or committee members' ability to function effectively.
(7)-(9) The arbitrator may order disclosure on limiting terms, considering any previous confidentiality breaches, and may order the right to disclosure withdrawn for a specified period in cases of breach.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Disputes concerning this Chapter
body:
(1) Any dispute about interpreting or applying this Chapter (other than disputes under sections 26(8) or 39) may be referred in writing to the Commission.
(3)-(4) The Commission must attempt conciliation, then arbitration if unresolved.
(5) The Labour Relations Act's arbitration provisions apply, with necessary changes.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Mine Health and Safety Council
body:
(1) The Council consists of five employer representatives, five employee representatives, four State department representatives, and the Chief Inspector of Mines who chairs it.
(2) The Minister appoints Council members in accordance with regulations.
(2A) The Council may appoint members to committees and subcommittees.
(3) The Council and its committees govern themselves per the constitution in section 97(3).
(4)-(5) The Council may delegate powers and assign duties in writing, subject to conditions, without preventing its own exercise of those powers.
(6) Council and committee members are entitled to have their views reflected in reports.
(7) The Minister, with Treasury agreement, must provide sufficient administrative funds annually.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Council's duties
body: The Council must advise the Minister on health and safety at mines (including mine rehabilitation legislation as it concerns health and safety), co-ordinate its committees' activities and liaise with the Mining Qualifications Authority, liaise with other relevant statutory bodies, promote a culture of health and safety, arrange a tripartite summit at least every two years to review the state of health and safety, annually advise the Minister on relevant research, and perform every duty imposed on it by this Act.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Mining Qualifications Authority
body:
(1) The Authority consists of five employer representatives, five employee representatives, four State department representatives, and the Chief Inspector of Mines who chairs it.
(2)-(3) Members are appointed and the Authority governs itself per the constitution in section 97(4).

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Mining Qualifications Authority's functions
body:
(1) The Authority must seek registration and accreditation under the South African Qualifications Authority Act, propose and generate education and training standards and qualifications in the mining industry, monitor and audit achievement against those standards, and perform sector education and training authority functions under the Skills Development Act.
(2) The Authority may appoint committees, must administer its finances per the Skills Development Act, and may do anything necessary to achieve its objectives.
(3)-(4) The Authority may delegate powers and assign duties in writing, subject to conditions.
(5) The Authority must comply with the South African Qualifications Authority's policies and criteria.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Chief Inspector of Mines
body:
(1) The Minister must appoint a suitably qualified and experienced officer as Chief Inspector of Mines.
(2) Subject to the Minister's control and direction, the Chief Inspector must perform the functions entrusted by this Act.
(3) The Chief Inspector may perform any function of an inspector.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Chief Inspector of Mines' functions
body:
(1) The Chief Inspector of Mines must ensure this Act is complied with and enforced, appoint a Medical Inspector and inspectors with prescribed qualifications, administer the Mine Health and Safety Inspectorate, determine and implement health and safety policies, consult the Council before issuing code of practice guidelines, collect and distribute health and safety information, advise the Minister, publish an annual plan of action, submit an annual report to the Minister, perform directed or prescribed duties, develop an integrated database and reporting system, conduct or commission research, and support the Council.
(2) The Chief Inspector must furnish a prescribed certificate to the Medical Inspector and each inspector.
(3) The Chief Inspector has power to monitor environmental aspects affecting health or safety, consulting the appropriate officer under mineral resources legislation.
(4) The Chief Inspector may enter agreements, authorise independent persons to act as inspectors, perform value-enhancing acts, require health and safety or hazard management systems, acquire or dispose of property, collaborate on training and information, provide financial training assistance, insure the Inspectorate, invest its money, and institute or defend legal action.
(5)-(6) The Chief Inspector must certify authorised persons and issue guidelines by Gazette notice.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Financial and judicial management of Mine Health and Safety Inspectorate
body:
(1) The Inspectorate's funds consist of parliamentary appropriations, donations, investment revenue, and money raised under this Act.
(2) The Inspectorate must use its funds to defray expenses from performing its functions.
(3) The Chief Inspector must, after consulting the Council, use monies collected under section 55B to promote health and safety in the mining industry.
(4) The Chief Inspector, as accounting authority, must open a bank account and deposit all received money.
(5) The Inspectorate may invest funds not immediately required, per any prescribed policy and Minister-approved manner.
(6) The Inspectorate's financial year runs 1 April to 31 March.
(7) The Chief Inspector's annual report must reflect the Inspectorate's financial affairs.
(8) The Inspectorate may not be placed under judicial management or liquidation except by a special Act of Parliament.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Co-operative governance
body:
(1) The Chief Inspector of Mines must co-ordinate the Inspectorate's functions with other organs of state regulating and promoting occupational health and safety, per the co-operative governance principles in Chapter 3 of the Constitution.
(2) The Chief Inspector may conclude co-operative agreements with relevant organs of state to give effect to this.

collection: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
title: Inspectors' powers
body:
(1) An inspector may enter any mine at any time without warrant, enter other places with a warrant, and bring in and use necessary vehicles, equipment, and material.
(2) While at a mine or place, an inspector may question any person, require document production and explanation, examine and copy documents, inspect articles/substances/machinery/work/conditions, inspect medical surveillance arrangements, seize documents or items, and perform other prescribed functions.
(3) An inspector may instruct any current or former employer, employee, or relevant person to appear for questioning.
(4)-(6) The employer may copy a document before seizure; an inspector may remove items for examination; a receipt must be issued for anything seized or removed.
